worked_solution:
The infimum of $B$ is the greatest lower bound of $B.$

To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $B$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

In our case, we have the following:

- Any number in the set $x\le \pi $ is smaller than or equal to the elements of $B.$ Thus, the set $(-\infty ,\pi ]$ contains only lower bounds of $B.$

- Any number in the set $x>\pi $ is **not** a lower bound of $B.$ In other words, we can always find an element of $B$ that is smaller than $x$ for any $x>\pi .$

Therefore, $(-\infty ,\pi ]$ is the set of lower bounds of $B,$ and

$$
inf(B)=max(-\infty ,\pi ]=\pi .
$$

Notice that $\pi \notin B.$

The completed reasoning is given below.

The infimum of $B$ is the $\text{greatest lower bound}$ of $B.$

The set of lower bounds of $B$ is as follows:

$$
\{x\in R\,:\,x\le \pi \}
$$

Therefore, $inf(B)=\pi \notin B.$
